publications.title: Elimination LArTPC Simulation Uncertainty With Modifcations to TPC Wire Waveforms
publications.subtitle: iNSPIRE
publications.description: This paper introduces a novel approach to reducing systematic uncertainties in LArTPC detector simulations, which arise from known detector effects that are challenging and computationally intensive to model. The proposed method involves modifying simulated waveforms based on observed discrepancies in ionization signals from the TPC between actual data and simulations. This approach reduces the sensitivity to detailed detector modeling and decreases the computational resources required for accurate simulations.

activity.title: Summit won audience choice at TroyLabs pitch night 🏔️🏔️ I keep thinking about how unlikely that sentence sounded a semester ago. I first met my co-founders Lucas Rival and Joseph Choi at USC's incubator LavaLab , where we spent nine weeks getting humbled. We pivoted more than any other team in the cohort. We found the idea for Summit after I tried to find my dad's business by asking ChatGPT for the best contractors. His story and his company weren't showing up in the fastest growing sales platform. We came back from spring break with two weeks left before demo day, and our pitch was so scrappy that we were almost blocked from the stage. The number of late nights and Red Bulls we went through... but it worked. We pitched, landed our first paying customer, and left LavaLab with something real. The following semester we got into Troylabs, USC's premier startup accelerator. The accelerator was a different game. We grew the team, got more chances to pitch in front of people who write actual checks, and Summit started feeling less like a project and more like a company. A huge part of that was the cracked TroyLabs people who joined us: Jennifer Zhang , Mihika Deshmukh, Matthew Wong , Carter Davis , Melanie Lee , Bryan Ramirez-Gonzalez , Maia Rocha , Dilen Kakar , and Mandy Guo . Nine people who bet on the future of marketing and made it real. Then pitch night came, and we walked away with the win. The check that came with it was technically the first money Summit has ever raised. We're now at 10x the monthly revenue we left LavaLab with. Our habit of pivoting never stopped, so we are still shipping new features. Couldn't have asked for better co-founders, teammates, and mentors!

Spent the last few days at ICLR 2026 in Rio 🇧🇷 We asked: when different LLMs learn the same task, do they solve it the same way internally? Spoiler: no. Qwen models use tight, localized circuits. Llama and Gemma distribute the same computation across way more components. The deeper takeaway: we're building increasingly powerful systems and still barely know what's happening inside them. Mech interp is one of the more honest attempts to fix that. Grateful to my co-authors Arya Bhardia , Julian Ramirez , and Syd Verma ! Paper: https://lnkd.in/ggKqPWKS see y'all at ACL 👋

“What’s the best way to write a LinkedIn post?” I asked ChatGPT. But while some of us are asking AI for writing advice, millions are asking it for best meal delivery services, astrology apps, or healthy sour candies. As AI becomes the new gateway to discovery, traditional SEO is fading. Companies now need new tools to keep their products on the top shelf of AI-generated responses. That's why we are building Summit through USC's premier incubator, LavaLab . Summit gives users the insights and actions they need to thrive in the age of AI search. Huge thanks to my teammates Joseph Choi , Lucas Rival , and Mohamed Amir Mamoon for all your hard work and great memories; our mentors Charles Gao , Bodie Currier , Xinyue Ma , and Rakshith Thuraga for all your energy and expertise; and the LavaLab E-board for making this semester exceptional. Last week we had the opportunity to pitch our product to 200+ attendees and three judges: Alex Leiman , Baylor Adams , and James Carlin . Now we are polishing our product, adding new features, and onboarding our first clients.

Thank you Bodie Currier , and our other exceptional mentors Xinyue Ma , Charles Gao , Rakshith Thuraga for bringing your experience, energy, and passion into our team! Grateful to work with greatest PM Lucas Rival , toughest designer Joseph Choi , and most cracked dev Mohamed Amir Mamoon on Summit.

Make the most of your college friends, because you might be stuck with them for a while. At least, that’s what the brilliant Steve Johnson (Head of design @ Netflix ) told us today during his unforgettable visit to LavaLab . But taking advantage of college years wasn’t the only wisdom that Steve shared as he dutifully answered a barrage of questions. Here are my top 3 takeaways: 1. Storytelling is your delta. When asked about how to stand out in today’s market, it wasn't any hard skill, but persuasion. If you can clearly articulate your vision and captivate an audience, you become invincible. This is what distinguishes great leaders and designers in today's market. Don't just do the work -- sell the vision. 2. Risky business is good business. Impactful achievements are made through bold action, not repeating old successes. You need to adopt a risk mindset and be willing to fail early and often, especially during your college years. It's cheesy but true: if you want a shot at breaking through the noise — both as a person and a company — you have to put something on the line. 3. Birds of a feather stick together. Steve described how throughout his career he has surrounded himself with the same friends and co-workers that drive success in every role. You will probably meet you lifelong co-workers and co-founders in college, if not right after. The most valuable thing you gain from college is the people you meet, so never stop meeting people. At Lavalab we share the very same belief in the importance of finding your co-founders in college. We couldn't be more thankful for your time and wisdom today, Steve Johnson !

Before I ever worked on propulsion hardware, I hid in my car during lunch breaks to watch Starship launches on my phone. At the time, I was working long nights waiting tables, taking classes at Dallas College , and trying to save enough money to keep moving toward an engineering degree. On launch days, I would duck into my tiny car, pull up Tim Dodd Everyday Astronaut livestream, and watch SpaceX send another rocket into the sky. I remember wondering what it must feel like to be part of something so transcendent. Those launches were more than something interesting to watch. They gave me a picture of the kind of work I wanted to spend my life pursuing. They fueled the stubborn part of me that refused to stop, even when college felt financially out of reach and the path into aerospace seemed impossibly far away. Today, I am incredibly proud and grateful to share that I will be spending Fall 2026 at SpaceX as an Engineering Intern with the Build Reliability team within Booster Propulsion Systems at Starbase. It is difficult to put into words what this opportunity means to the version of me sitting in that car. This is not a finish line, and I am not arriving as a finished engineer. I have been given the opportunity to spend a semester learning from an extraordinary team and doing what I love most: working closely with hardware, contributing wherever I can, and continuing to build the engineer I plan to become. To my husband, my family, and every professor, mentor, teammate, and friend who helped me keep going, thank you. I did not make it here alone, and I will never forget the people who helped me believe this was possible. I am proud of that girl years ago who refused to give up, grateful for everyone who helped her keep moving, and I'm ready to learn everything I can. We're taking on a new group of R&D interns at our Yerevan office this September, and we'd love for you to apply! Six months, paid, part-time, onsite. We'll get to the requirements — but first, the part that's more fun to talk about: what you'd actually be working on (yes, we expect interns to do real, meaningful work). Deep Origin builds computational drug discovery infrastructure. AI, scientific computing, and quantum chemistry, all pointed at the same stubborn problem: discovery programs run for years, and most of them fail anyway. We're trying to get that down to months. It's a big goal, and we're not shy about saying it's hard. A few programs and product areas we're proud of: 🧪 Advanced Research + Invention Agency (ARIA) picked us — together with Arctoris — for its AI Scientist program. That's an autonomous research agent working on endometriosis, a condition affecting roughly 190 million people that still has no approved disease-modifying drug. And the agent does its thinking out loud: 10,539 papers pulled into an evidence lake, 323 candidate targets extracted, eventually narrowed to 3. The dead ends get published too, which is the part we like most. 🧪 We're building predictive ADME-Tox models through the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health (ARPA-H) Catalyst program. 🧪 And we're building a platform for the future of drug discovery. Balto, DO Patent, and DO Studio are all live and free to try. Feel free to poke around before you apply, it's a great way to quickly explore the problem spaces we're working in. Here's how we think about internships: they are equally about learning and contributing. So you'll get a dedicated mentor, code review on everything you write, weekly seminars and tech talks from engineers and researchers across the company, and a genuine shot at co-authoring a paper. The projects are real ones, not busywork invented to keep you occupied. And for the people it works out with, there's a full-time offer at the end. To view the requirements and full job description check out the link below! https://lnkd.in/gDMffy-Y

This summer, I had the incredible opportunity to participate in NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration ’s Student Airborne Research Program (SARP)! Over the course of the program, I flew aboard several NASA research aircraft, including the Langley G-III equipped with GCAS and AWP, the Langley G-V with HSRL-2, and the Armstrong G-III with UAVSAR. Seeing these instruments operate in the field was one of the highlights of the summer. I also participated in fieldwork around Galveston Bay, collecting data with the University of Houston’s mobile air quality laboratory and research vessel and launching weather balloons equipped with radiosondes and ozonesondes. Another highlight was working with some of my peers to prepare and deliver a weather forecast briefing for SARP flight operations. This gave me a firsthand look at how meteorology, instrumentation, and mission planning come together during an airborne campaign. For my research project, I used airborne LiDAR observations from AWP and HALO to investigate mountain wave signatures in the atmosphere. This project introduced me to atmospheric dynamics from a remote sensing perspective and made me especially excited about the potential of airborne LiDAR to observe processes that may be difficult to fully resolve using models or satellites alone! SARP was incredibly impactful in helping me clarify the direction I hope to take in Earth science and remote sensing, but more than anything, I am grateful to my mentors, program staff, and everyone in SARP East and West who made this experience so meaningful. A special shout-out to my Atmosphere East group: Hannah Akel , Zayna Haider , Samantha (Sammy) Lee , Matthew Simpson , and Kiaya McCuin! Thank you to my faculty mentors, Mary Angelique G. Demetillo and Dan Goldberg , my graduate mentor, Leo Bloxham , and the AWP and HALO PIs, Kristopher Bedka and Amin Nehrir , for their guidance and support throughout my project. Finally, thank you to Cynthia Hall , Yaítza Luna-Cruz, Ph.D., Joelle Hopkins , ECR, and everyone who supported the program. I am incredibly thankful for this summer and so excited to carry these experiences forward!
